subject: Cognitive Science
title: Essentialist Thinking
description: A fast breakdown of Essentialist Thinking for builders.

hook.text: People feel a sweater once worn by a killer is "contaminated." They sense an invisible essence.

buildup.text: Psychological essentialism is the belief that categories have a hidden inner nature that makes them real.

discovery.text: Susan Gelman found that even preschoolers think animals have an internal essence that determines behavior.

twist.text: Essentialism works for gold (it really has an atomic essence) but fails for race or gender.

climax.text: Treating social categories as "natural kinds" fuels discrimination by making groups feel fixed.

punchline.text: Not every category has a hidden essence.

quiz.question: What is psychological essentialism?
options: The belief that categories have a hidden inner nature
The idea that all categories are artificial

details.summary: Psychological essentialism is the belief that categories have hidden inner essences that make members what they are. People assume a tiger has an invisible tigriness even if it loses its stripes. Essentialism helps organize biological categories but leads to trouble when applied to social groups.
details.whyItMatters: Essentialism is a cognitive default that shapes how people think about race, gender, and nationality. Recognizing it helps explain stereotyping and prejudice.
takeaways: People assume categories have hidden essences
Essentialism works for biology but misleads for social groups
It drives the belief that category membership is fixed and deep

faq.question: Why is essentialism problematic for social categories?
faq.answer: When people essentialize race, gender, or nationality, they assume group members share a fixed inner nature. This leads to rigid stereotyping and the belief that group differences are natural and unchangeable. Social categories are culturally constructed and do not have biological essences.

faq.question: Do children show essentialist thinking?
faq.answer: Yes. By age four, children expect that a baby raised by a different species will still develop its birth species' traits. They assume a crocodile egg hatched by a duck will grow into a reptile, not a bird. This early essentialism shows it is a cognitive default, not a taught belief.
